phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b] followed by the diphthong [ai] or [aja]. The first syllable carries the stress in the most common English scholarly reading.
Open central vowel [a]; in some traditions this is a light, unstressed syllable between the stressed first and final syllables.
Final unstressed syllable [mi] or [me], often interpreted as the root for 'maker' or 'father' in southeastern Australian languages.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BYE-ah-meh' — stress the first syllable, keep the vowels open, and avoid turning the final vowel into a long English 'ee'.

kin.label: Gamilaraay / Euahlayi
kin.form: Baayami, the maker or father figure recorded by K. Langloh Parker in The Euahlayi Tribe (1905)

kin.label: Wiradjuri
kin.form: Baiame / Byamee, the Sky Father and creator widely attested in central New South Wales

kin.label: Daramulum
kin.form: The son or mediator of Baiame, often associated with weather, the rainbow, and initiation rites

pronunciation.note: The name Baiame is a romanization of an oral tradition; no single original script exists. PuniCodex renders it as Baiame, capitalizing the conventional scholarly citation form. Because the restoration does not add a diacritic or distinctive letter absent from the ASCII form, the name is Tier 2. The spoken name and the mythic role remain intact; the ASCII string is a DNS convenience, not an ancient spelling.

domains.title: Sky Father and Maker
domains.subtitle: Creator, Law-Giver, and Ancestor
domains.lead: Baiame is the great creator and Sky Father of several Aboriginal nations of south-eastern Australia, above all the Wiradjuri and the Gamilaraay/Euahlayi. He made the land, the animals, and the people, and then gave them the laws, kinship systems, and initiation ceremonies by which they still live. After the work of creation he withdrew to the sky, where he remains as a remote but watchful ancestor, his presence felt in the Milky Way, in the flight of the emu, and in the sound of the bullroarer at initiation.

cards.name: Creator of Land and Life
cards.desc: Baiame shaped the mountains, rivers, and plains, and made the first people and animals. Creation is not a single event but an ongoing relationship with country.

cards.name: Sky Dwelling
cards.desc: After creation Baiame returned to the sky. His camp is sometimes identified with the dark patches and stars of the Milky Way, especially the Emu in the Sky.

cards.name: Law and Initiation
cards.desc: He gave the first laws, the kinship rules, and the initiation ceremonies that turn boys into men. The bullroarer is sounded in his name.

cards.name: Great Ancestor
cards.desc: Baiame is not worshipped in the everyday sense; he is remembered as the founding ancestor whose actions set the moral and social order of the world.

symbols.name: The Emu in the Sky
symbols.meaning: The dark constellation of the Milky Way, a celestial marker of Baiame's camp and of the emu he created

symbols.name: Bullroarer
symbols.meaning: A sacred sound-maker used in men's initiation; its voice is associated with Baiame and his son Daramulum

symbols.name: Stone arrangements and bora rings
symbols.meaning: Earth-and-stone ceremonial sites where initiation and law are enacted under Baiame's authority

symbols.name: Stone axes
symbols.meaning: Often linked to Baiame as tools of creation and as sacred objects exchanged across southeast Australia

mythology.lead: Baiame's mythology is preserved in the oral traditions of the Wiradjuri, Gamilaraay, and neighbouring nations. The stories are not free-floating entertainment: they are title deeds to country, instruction manuals for law, and maps of the sky. What follows are widely reported themes; local elders hold the authoritative versions of each nation's stories.

myths.title: The Making of the World
myths.text: In the beginning Baiame shaped the land. He formed the hills and rivers, planted the trees, and made the animals. Then he made the first people and gave them their languages, their countries, and the laws by which they should live. Every mountain, waterhole, and plain became a reminder of his creative act, and every clan received the responsibility to care for the part of country made for them.

myths.title: The Retreat to the Sky
myths.text: When the work of creation was finished, Baiame rose into the sky and made his camp there. From that distant place he watches over the world he made. The dark lanes of the Milky Way are said to be his camp or the tracks of the emu he placed there; the stars themselves are the campfires of the ancestors who went before.

myths.title: The Son Daramulum
myths.text: Baiame's son Daramulum moves between earth and sky as a messenger and teacher. Often associated with the rainbow and with thunder, Daramulum taught the people the secrets of initiation and the songs that must be sung at each stage of life. Through him, Baiame's law is passed on without the Sky Father needing to descend himself.

myths.title: The Emu in the Sky
myths.text: The dark shape of the emu stretches across the Milky Way. It is both a constellation and a story: the emu in the sky tells the people when to collect emu eggs, when to hold ceremonies, and how to read the seasons. Baiame placed it there as a calendar and a memory, so that the connection between sky and country would never be lost.

etymology.derivation: The name is generally understood as 'the maker' or 'father' in the languages of the Wiradjuri and Gamilaraay/Euahlayi peoples. Older transcriptions render it as Byamee or Baayami. The exact pre-contact form cannot be recovered with certainty because the name was transmitted orally and only written down in colonial times.

cognates.note: The Euahlayi/Gamilaraay form recorded by K. Langloh Parker
The central New South Wales form, often paired with Birrahgnooloo and Daramulum

nameVariations.note: Standard scholarly and PuniCodex restoration; the most widely used romanization.
Gamilaraay/Euahlayi spelling used by Parker (1905) and in contemporary language revival.
Older colonial transcription, now less common in scholarly use.
Functional glosses used when the name itself is treated as a title rather than a personal name.

syncretism: Early colonial observers sometimes compared Baiame to the Christian God, and some recorded traditions show signs of post-contact reinterpretation. Modern scholarship, led by Berndt and Berndt and by AIATSIS, treats Baiame as a specifically Aboriginal Sky Father whose identity is tied to country, kinship, and initiation rather than to any universal deity. He is not interchangeable with the biblical creator, and each nation retains its own protocols for how his name and stories may be used.
culturalLegacy: Baiame remains a powerful symbol of Aboriginal sovereignty over country and culture. His name appears in place names, in rock art and stencil sites, and in contemporary Aboriginal art and literature. The Emu in the Sky is now widely recognised as one of the best-known Aboriginal astronomical traditions. At the same time, Aboriginal custodians have rightly insisted that Baiame's sacred aspects — especially those connected with men's law and initiation — are not open-source material for casual adaptation. PuniCodex presents only the publicly documented, scholarly record and directs readers to AIATSIS and to the relevant Aboriginal communities for authoritative teachings.
extendedMeditation:
Baiame asks the modern reader to think about creation as responsibility. The world is not a finished product handed to humanity; it is a country made by an ancestor and entrusted to his descendants. To speak the name Baiame is therefore to remember a covenant: the land, the water, the animals, and the sky are kin, and the law that governs them is older than any statute.

That is why the restoration matters. The plain ASCII form flattens the name into a string of letters with no memory of the languages that carried it. The Unicode restoration Baiame does not add diacritics, because the original sources were oral, but it does reclaim the capitalized, scholarly citation form by which the figure is named in museums, universities, and Aboriginal-studies curricula. The name is Tier 2 not because it is less important, but because the DNS-friendly ASCII form already encodes the same phonemic sequence. The work of preservation here is cultural and historical, not diacritical.
originalScriptNote: Baiame belongs to an oral tradition that had no pre-contact writing system. The name first enters the written record in nineteenth-century ethnographies. PuniCodex therefore restores it as Baiame, the conventional capitalized romanization, rather than as an 'original script' in the strict sense. The ASCII form baiame is a practical DNS compromise; the restored form is the scholarly citation form used in Australian Indigenous studies.

archaeology: The material record of Baiame-related belief includes stone arrangements, bora (initiation) grounds, rock engravings, and rock shelters across the Wiradjuri and Gamilaraay countries of New South Wales. Notable sites include Baiame Cave near Milbrodale in the Hunter Valley, which contains a large painted figure sometimes identified with Baiame, and numerous carved and painted emus that reference the Emu in the Sky. These sites are protected under Aboriginal cultural-heritage law and are best understood in consultation with the traditional custodians.
